Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

for first-time players. The event was scheduled for October 12 and 13 at the Old Ferry Hall, and the organizers expected about 80 people. The hall had a main room with 12 tables, a smaller room beside the kitchen, and a narrow entrance where people would need to collect their badges. The tournament director was Mara Ellis, and the volunteer coordinating the check-in desk was Tomas Reed.

The first issue was that the registration page listed two different closing dates. The top of the page said entries would close on September 28, while the paragraph at the bottom said September 30. Mara told me the later date was correct because she had moved the deadline after the city extended the hall booking. She had not updated the first line yet, so I wrote down that the page needed one date, not that either date had been confirmed by the website team. The entry fee was 32 pounds for adults and 20 pounds for players under 18. The fee included lunch on both days but not accommodation. People could ask for a reduced fee by emailing the organizers, and the page said requests would be considered individually. It did not state an income threshold or promise that a request would be accepted.

Section One: Details to verify before opening the desk

1. The player list should show each entrant’s name, club if supplied, rating, and requested section.
2. The desk should have printed receipts for cash payments and a separate envelope for card terminal slips.
3. The organizers needed a clear process for a player whose payment appeared twice in the online account. Tomas said he had seen duplicate notices before but did not know whether both charges had actually settled.
4. The notices should explain that players had to tell the organizers about a withdrawal by email rather than assume a message in the tournament chat counted as formal notice.

I asked whether the chat could be used for quick questions, and Mara said, “It is fine for directions and arrival updates, but I still need the withdrawal in my inbox.”

The entry form asked for a full name, a contact email, a club when applicable, and a rating as of September 1. It also asked players to choose the Open or the Under 16 section. The Under 16 event required the player to be younger than 16 on the first day. There was no separate girls’ section and no junior prize listed outside that event. Mara said they would accept an unrated player but would ask for a short note about recent games so that the pairings could be checked. She did not say that an unrated player would be placed in a particular rating band. The form had a box for accessibility requests and a separate field for dietary needs; both were optional. The kitchen could provide vegetarian and dairy-free lunches, but Mara was still checking whether the caterer could handle a severe nut allergy.

I sat with Tomas at the hall one afternoon, and we walked through the route from the entrance to the desk. The first table was close to the door, but the queue could block the fire exit if it turned toward the coat hooks. The hall manager had asked them to keep a meter of clear space in front of that exit and had marked the area with blue tape. The smaller room could hold a waiting line, but it was also where the organizers planned to store clocks and spare sets. Tomas suggested putting the sign-in desk along the long wall and keeping one volunteer at the door to guide arrivals. No one had yet checked whether the tables would leave enough room for a wheelchair to pass between the registration area and the main playing room. The hall manager said they could move two tables if needed but asked for the final layout by the Monday before the tournament.

We also reviewed what players would receive after checking in. The packet was expected to include a name badge, a printed schedule, a hall map, and a small card with the tournament contact number. The schedule showed round one at 10:30 on Saturday and round five at 10 on Sunday, with later rounds listed as approximate times because the director wanted to allow for long games. Mara planned to post pairings on a board near the main room and on the event page. The page did not promise text alerts, and some participants had asked whether pairings would be available through an app. Tomas said they could not commit to that unless someone tested the software with the final player list. He had a spreadsheet from last year, but the old list included contact details and could not simply be shared with this year’s volunteers.

There were practical questions about arriving and paying as well. The nearest bus stop was on Quay Road, and the hall had a small car park that was shared with the library. After six o’clock, the library staff expected fewer visitors but had not reserved spaces for the tournament. One player had asked whether overnight parking was allowed, and Mara had referred the question to the hall manager rather than guessing. The organizers could take card payments through a handheld terminal or cash at the desk, but did not want volunteers to accept bank transfers into personal accounts. Tomas had drafted a cash count sheet with columns for the amount received, the receipt number, and the initials of the volunteer who counted it. Mara asked him to add a place to record a refund if one was issued before the entry deadline.

On Friday evening, the team planned to place signs from the Quay Road entrance to the hall door and check that the room was unlocked before setting up. They would bring extension leads, two spare clocks, a first aid kit, and paper copies of the contact list. The list was meant for the organizers and would include only the phone numbers volunteers needed during the event. The director wanted the public schedule to show when the desk opened and when late arrivals should contact a volunteer, but had not decided whether the desk would remain staffed through every round. I wrote down that we should not print the signs until the hall manager confirmed the route because the side entrance might be closed for maintenance on Saturday morning.

When I finished the notes, Mara asked me to send her the list of page changes and the unresolved questions. She said she wanted the deadline corrected first, then the allergy information checked with the caterer, and the room layout reviewed with the hall manager. She had not asked me to edit the public page, and I did not have access to its account. I could send the notes to Tomas as well because he was preparing the desk supplies, but the player list was still being updated and the volunteers had not agreed who would receive the final version.
